h1: Writing a brew day timeline so nothing gets rushed
title: Writing a Brew Day Timeline | Craft Beer School
desc: How to write a brew day timeline that counts back from pitching, with real durations for heating, mashing, boiling, chilling and cleaning.
teaser: Most brew day mistakes happen in the last two hours. A written timeline moves the panic to the night before, where it costs nothing.
standfirst: An all-grain brew day runs five to seven hours and the hard parts all arrive at once. A timeline written the night before tells you what is coming next. Here is how we build one.
sections: Rushed steps cause most brew day faults

Ask any homebrewer about their worst batch and the story usually starts with a rush. The hop addition went in ten minutes late because the sparge was still running. The chiller was not sanitised because the boil finished early. The yeast was pitched warm because it was midnight and everyone wanted to sleep.

None of these are knowledge problems. The brewer knew what to do. They simply ran out of attention at the moment it mattered. A typical all-grain day on a 20 litre system takes five to seven hours from lighting the burner to the last clean bucket. Writing that time down in order is the cheapest quality tool in brewing.
Work backwards from the moment you pitch

Start the timeline at the end. Pick the time you want the yeast in the fermenter, then subtract each stage. For a first all-grain batch on a gas stove, these durations are realistic:

  • Heating strike water for a 20 litre batch: 30 to 45 minutes.
  • Mash: 60 minutes, plus 10 for a mash out if you do one.
  • Lautering and sparging: 30 to 60 minutes depending on method.
  • Bringing the wort to a boil: 20 to 40 minutes.
  • Boil: 60 minutes, or 90 for a pale lager made with Pilsner malt.
  • Chilling: 20 to 40 minutes, longer in summer.
  • Transfer, aeration and pitching: 20 minutes.

Add those up and you are at roughly five and a half hours before cleaning. If you want to pitch by 6 pm, the burner goes on before 12:30. Most people who skip this sum discover it at 11 pm.

Brew in a bag cuts the lautering stage to a few minutes of lifting and draining, so take 30 to 45 minutes off. Extract brewing removes the mash entirely. Whatever your method, use your own numbers once you have them. A 25 litre pot on a domestic gas ring heats far slower than a 3,500 watt electric system.
Turn the boil into a countdown

Recipes list hop additions as minutes remaining: 60, 15, 5, flame out. Under pressure it is easy to misread that as minutes elapsed. Write the boil as clock times instead. If the boil starts at 3:10 pm, the bittering hops go in at 3:10, the 15 minute addition at 3:55 and the flame-out hops at 4:10.

Put everything that happens late in the boil on the same list. Kettle finings at 15 minutes. The immersion chiller into the kettle at 15 minutes so the boil sanitises it. Yeast out of the fridge an hour before pitching so it is not shocked by warm wort. These jobs are small. Forgetting one ruins a batch.

Give each late job a tick box. When the boil is rolling, steam fogs your glasses and someone is asking what smells of porridge, a tick box is easier to trust than memory.
Schedule the jobs that hide between stages

The gaps are where a good timeline earns its keep. The 60 minute mash is not dead time. It is when you heat sparge water to around 75 to 78 °C, weigh hops into labelled cups and mix sanitiser. The boil is when you clean the mash tun, because spent grain sets like cement in a few hours of Indian heat.

Sanitising also needs time on the plan. Every no-rinse sanitiser has a contact time on its label. Write when the fermenter gets filled with sanitiser so it has done its job before the wort arrives. Our guide to a first all-grain brew day walks through the stages in more detail.
Build in a buffer for heat, gas and water

Real brew days run long. In an Indian summer, tap water comes out at 28 to 32 °C. An immersion chiller cannot take wort below that without ice, so chilling often doubles. An LPG cylinder can run out mid-boil. A stuck sparge can add half an hour.

We add 30 minutes of buffer to every timeline and park it after chilling. If the day runs to plan, you finish early. If it does not, the delay eats the buffer instead of your pitching temperature. Keep a spare cylinder or a full one booked before brew day. Freeze water bottles two days ahead if the forecast is above 30 °C.
Compare the plan with what happened

A timeline is half a document until you write actual times beside planned ones. After three or four brews you will know your own numbers: how long your burner takes to heat 25 litres, how much your kettle evaporates in an hour, how long your chiller takes in May versus December. Those numbers make the next timeline accurate instead of hopeful.

Keep the timeline inside your brew log so plan and result sit together. Where the gap between them is biggest, that is the stage to improve first. Understanding why each step takes the time it does is where a structured course pays off over trial and error.

You do not need software. Take your next recipe and a sheet of paper. Write the pitch time at the bottom and work upwards, stage by stage, using the durations above. Mark every hop addition as a clock time. Add the side jobs in the gaps. Then put 30 minutes of buffer after chilling.

Stick the sheet on the wall near the stove. On brew day, write the real time next to each line as you go. That one sheet will teach you more about your system than any calculator.
faqs: How long does an all-grain brew day take?
On a typical 20 litre homebrew setup, five to seven hours including cleaning. Brew in a bag on a single pot can be an hour or so shorter.
Should hop additions be written as minutes remaining or clock times?
Recipes give minutes remaining in the boil. On brew day, convert them to clock times from the moment the boil starts so you cannot misread them under pressure.
What is the most common timing mistake?
Underestimating chilling in hot weather. Warm tap water slows an immersion chiller a lot, so plan ice or extra time in summer.
